title: RC Charging: The Time Constant τ = RC
hook: How fast does a capacitor charge? The answer is hidden in the product of R and C.

equation.caption: Capacitor voltage during charging in a series RC circuit.

steps: The time constant is \(\tau = RC = {{R}} \times {{C}} = {{tau}}\) s.
The capacitor voltage follows \(V(t) = V_0 (1 - e^{-t/\tau})\).

explorations.title: Effect of R on charging time
explorations.predict: If you double R, what happens to the time to reach 63% of V₀?
explorations.observe: The curve rises more slowly. The time constant τ = RC doubles, so it takes twice as long to reach the same fraction of V₀.
explorations.why: Because τ = RC, increasing R increases τ, which stretches the exponential curve in time.

explorations.title: Voltage at one time constant
explorations.predict: What is V(τ) as a fraction of V₀?
explorations.observe: At t = τ, the voltage is about 63.2% of V₀.
explorations.why: Substituting t = τ into V(t) = V₀(1 - e^{-t/τ}) gives V(τ) = V₀(1 - e^{-1}) ≈ 0.632 V₀.

limitation: This model assumes an ideal voltage source, ideal resistor, and ideal capacitor with no parasitic elements. It does not account for the internal resistance of the source or the equivalent series resistance (ESR) of the capacitor, which can affect the charging time in real circuits.
misconception: Many think the capacitor charges linearly. In reality, the charging follows an exponential curve, and the rate slows down as the capacitor voltage approaches the supply voltage.

claims.text: The time constant τ is the product of resistance and capacitance: τ = RC.
The capacitor voltage during charging is given by V(t) = V₀(1 - e^{-t/τ}).
After one time constant, the capacitor reaches approximately 63.2% of the supply voltage.
After five time constants, the capacitor is considered fully charged (over 99%).
In our simulation, we assume ideal components and a constant voltage source, ignoring parasitic resistances and inductances.

outcomes.outcome: Explain the meaning of the time constant τ = RC.
Sketch the exponential charging curve V(t) = V₀(1 - e^{-t/τ}).
Calculate the voltage at t = τ and t = 5τ.
Verify that V(0) = 0 and V(τ) ≈ 0.632 V₀.
